claims.text: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a single-phase fcc matrix.
The as-built alloy has a uniform elemental distribution.
The initial microstructure and elemental distribution are optimized for strength and fatigue performance.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by competition between protective surface-scale formation and internal oxidation with elemental segregation.
Under oxidizing conditions, the protective scale forms predominantly through oxidation of Al and Cr.
The protective oxide scale is coherent or adherent.
Reducing exposure promotes internal oxidation and elemental segregation, particularly involving Ti.
Exposure atmosphere controls the evolution of Al2O3 and Cr-containing surface oxides.
Oxide-scale evolution produces associated near-surface elemental depletion and segregation profiles.
Under oxidizing conditions, a protective oxide layer forms rapidly and subsequently grows slowly.
The protective oxide layer limits further elemental diffusion and degradation.
Under reducing conditions, insufficient protective-scale formation permits internal oxidation.
Internal oxidation and Ti enrichment or depletion undermine the alloy's microstructural integrity.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a uniform protective scale and preserve mechanical properties relative to the as-built baseline.
Reducing exposure will cause more internal oxidation and elemental segregation than oxidizing exposure.
Reducing exposure will increase porosity relative to the as-built baseline.
Reducing exposure will produce degradation at grain boundaries relative to the as-built baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies over 750–900 °C and exposure durations of 10–100 hours.
Conditions outside 750–900 °C and 10–100 hours may activate alternative degradation mechanisms.
